where: Exam traps, bullet 2, and Quiz Q5 (question and answer)
problem: The example XSS value is given as alert(1). A bare text value alert(1) printed inside HTML does nothing — it is not script, so the stated output ('the browser runs it as script') is wrong. A student would learn the wrong payload and the wrong reason for escaping.
fix: Use a real payload: a name like <script>alert(1)</script> (or "><script>alert(1)</script> if it lands inside an attribute) is printed as markup, so the browser runs it as script. Say: without htmlspecialchars the < and > are sent as characters and the browser treats the value as markup, not text.

problem: filter_input(INPUT_POST, 'marks', FILTER_VALIDATE_INT) is said to return an integer or false. It also returns null when the key is not present in the request at all, which is exactly why the worked example tests === null. The stated rule and the code disagree.
fix: Say: returns the integer when the value is a valid integer, false when the value is present but not a valid integer, and null when the field is missing. Check for null as well as false.

where: Section 2, second paragraph, and Exam traps, bullet 1
problem: The text says $_REQUEST merges GET, POST and cookies and that 'a cookie can override a form field'. The merge order actually comes from the request_order setting, and in the standard php.ini files request_order is 'GP', so cookies are normally not in $_REQUEST at all; the clash is usually GET overriding POST.
fix: Say: $_REQUEST merges GET, POST and (depending on the request_order setting) cookies, in an order set by configuration. With the common default order 'GP' a query-string value overrides a POST value of the same name, and cookies are left out. Read $_GET or $_POST instead.

problem: Idempotent is defined as 'repeating the same GET should not change data'. That is the definition of a safe method. Idempotent means repeating the request has the same effect on the server as sending it once.
fix: Say: a GET is safe (it should not change data on the server) and idempotent (sending it twice leaves the server in the same state as sending it once). POST is neither safe nor idempotent in general.

problem: The figure shows the GET returning '200 HTML Anu scored 78', but the script in Worked example 1 only processes POST; on a GET it returns the form. The caption 'The server returns the same HTML for both' contradicts the chapter's own code and its self-submit rule.
fix: Either label the figure as a generic illustration of where the pairs travel, or change the GET response to '200 HTML the form' and keep '200 HTML Anu scored 78' for the POST, matching the self-submit pattern taught in Section 2.

problem: The body is written as 'body name=Anu marks=78', without the & between the pairs, while the rest of the chapter uses name=Anu&marks=78. The figure is the one place a student may copy the format from.
fix: Write the message as 'body name=Anu&marks=78' (Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded).

where: Section 3, last paragraph, and Quiz Q2 answer
problem: The text explains why GET is bad for a password but never says that a POST body is also readable on the wire unless the connection is HTTPS. A reader can conclude that POST alone makes a password safe.
fix: Add one line: POST hides the password from the URL, history and logs, but the body is plain text on the network; use HTTPS so the whole request is encrypted.
